utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Sarah Clanton; case manager, Thomas Laugel; and legal interns, Sarah Munsch and Katherine Davis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell with Adam Harnischfeger, intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, you probably that you're at about 20 hours of your examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, you remember last Thursday we discussed your talks with Mr. Wijnaendts on 12 October 1991 in Paris, and I will now show you a document reflecting another conversation you had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is 1D3033. It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Tab number 1127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I won't read to you the whole text of this document, but I've noticed that Mr. Babic took the floor at that meeting. It's not recorded that you said anything yourself. Could you tell us, first of all, is that correct; and, if so, for what reason?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and the reason is simple. As I said last time, at the meeting in Paris that took place at the Dutch embassy, I had talks with Mr. Wijnaendts where he conveyed to me the positions of the European Union and their proposals to us. And I said it was acceptable to me but it needs to be discussed with Mr. Babic because I can't accept in case he refuses, that that would put me into a lot of trouble, and that's why I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence, 1D3033, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D136, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you recall that after that conference, a press conference was held and you spoke at that press conference?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, but I think it was towards the end of that month. I'm not sure that it was during the conference, but I remember the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D602, please. It is tab -- it is tab 775.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you recall maybe this article published in the newspaper?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That press conference took place just after we returned, although later there was another one, so I thought you maybe mean that one. But I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you said here: We can't join Serbia because people had declared themselves in favour of staying within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said the most acceptable option is the one involving special status. Were those your words?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were my words, and we in Slavonia, Baranja were prepared to discuss a special status, but certain preconditions had to be met, and it couldn't happen overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence, 1D602.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D137, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D144, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is tab 732. It is page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another statement you made after negotiations with Mr. Wijnaendts, and you say, among other things: We represent the will of the people and we cannot be too flexible. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, these things could not happen overnight. If you take into account the fact that we had had a referendum where almost 100 per cent of the Serbian people declared themselves in favour of staying within Yugoslavia and the fact that I had to represent the will of the majority, as well as the position of my Assembly on that issue, so I didn't have much room. But if things had been resolved in a peaceful situation, it could have been handled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence. It is 1D144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you remember that another round of talks were supposed to take place with Mr. Wijnaendts and then were cancelled for some reason; and if you remember it, then tell us when did that happen.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that another round of talks had been planned, but after all this time I can't be 100 per cent sure, I believe it was in the beginning of October, when Mr. Babic refused to go for those talks, so I had no other option. But, anyway, since they were not inviting me alone anymore, we had to wait for another chance. I was not invited alone, on my own, anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1174. It is tab 302.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an allegedly intercepted conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic. Only the first two pages are relevant for our purposes. You probably remember the contents. And you see that Milosevic is expressing his dissatisfaction to Karadzic; I believe it's on page 2. We see, among other things, that just at the beginning of page 2, Radovan Karadzic says: "They didn't go." It says Misa Milosevic would be representing them over there. Can you remember this? But, first of all, tell me, as far as can you see, does this conversation relate precisely your travel to that scheduled talk with Mr. Wijnaendts?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Judging by the date, this intercept was recorded on the 9th of October, and your talks were scheduled for the 8th; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this intercept was made on the 8th and the talks were scheduled for an earlier time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you now what was the reason why you were supposed to go to those talks with Mr. Wijnaendts in the first place? Was it on your own initiative or somebody else's?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the idea of Mr. Wijnaendts and the people from the European Community at that time. It was not our initiative. Later on, talks in The Hague were scheduled, and I believe there was a conference scheduled to include all the representatives of the SFRY, and we were supposed to have a meeting with them separately before that conference. Then a problem occurred because of Mr. Ahrens and his conference and their negotiations with Ibrahim Rugova. I didn't quite understand why Mr. Ahrens would be a problem or why they were talking to Rugova. However, he drew some political implications from that because they were talking to Albanians as a minority and then by implication we were also supposed to be treated as a minority. I didn't understand any of it, but that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you express any misgivings about getting involved in those negotiations in view of your lack of experience in international negotiations and was anything done about it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was aware that I couldn't just show up and negotiate about such things considering that I was clueless. I must stress that Mr. Babic had contacts with some people in the diaspora and one faction of the opposition in Belgrade and he was receiving information that I didn't have, such as that Ahrens would be talking to Rugova. But within the federal state of which we were still a part, I wanted to talk to some people who would instruct me as to how these international negotiations work and how they are led and who could teach me a bit. That's why I talked to experts from the Academy of Arts and Science who were acting in a non-partisan way and who gave me some technical instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it some sort of preparations and how long could that have lasted? How much of your time did that take up?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call it preparations, and it lasted throughout the month of October. I had these talks with them when I first went for the preparations, and when I returned I stated the conclusions, how you can ask questions, how you act in a diplomatic manner, all sort of things that I knew nothing about at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And where were these preparations held? In which place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the preparations took place in Belgrade, either at the Serbian government or on the ground floor of the Presidency of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who informed you or invited you to these negotiations? Did international negotiators contact you directly or was it someone from the then-Yugoslav or Serbian government who did that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we received that both from the secretary of President Milosevic and from the federal government's protocol office, I'm not sure. And it depended on the occasion. But we received information from both these sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now that we dealt with intercepts, I am going to show you another one in which your name is mentioned. It does not deal with international negotiations but, rather, with something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 2806. It is tab 1307. It is P2806.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a conversation which you can see on the first side it was recorded on the 14th of December, 1991, a conversation between Jovica Stanisic, on the one hand, and Radovan Karadzic. They discuss some events in Banja Luka. Some figures are discussed, numbers. I'm not sure what exactly that -- those figures concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is interesting for us is page 3 of this document, both in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is stated that Jovica says that it was difficult for him to persuade you not to go there, and Banja Luka is mentioned. I wonder whether you remember if you had intended for any reason to go to Banja Luka in December?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a completely crazy assumption. It never occurred to me nor did I ever think about it. I did not have anything to do there and I don't know who I would get in touch there in the first place. I don't know what sort of game is at stake here and how come that my name figures here, but you can see how Radovan Karadzic reacted. He asked three times who it was, and he couldn't believe that my name had anything to do with these events and what I would be doing there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the alleged words are here. I cannot claim whether it really was like that or not. But allegedly Jovica, let's suppose it's Stanisic, says that it was difficult for him and he hardly managed to convince you not to go there. Did you have any contacts with him then in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no contacts with Jovica Stanisic in 1991, nor am I aware of the context in which this is inserted here. I had the occasion when I received these materials last year to ask Mr. Karadzic about this. He told me that it had nothing to do with me, and he said that he would be replacing some of his SDS members in the Banja Luka region and that he had no idea how this came to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could just tell us what is your answer to the question whether at the time you talked with Jovica Stanisic at all.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said clearly that I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember from the evidence that we've had occasion to see here that in the month of October, people moved out from Ilok in great numbers. Those were the ethnic Croatian citizens. I'm interested in this: Did you participate in the negotiations prior to the moving out of Croats and other non-Serbs from Ilok and the surrounding places?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate at all. All the information I had came from the media. I had expected to be invited to assist and to talk, but nobody called me and nobody contacted me. But I believe that it would have been logical to invite me as Ilok was part of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P321. It is tab 234. May we see page 3 in B/C/S; page 4 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of the instances of minutes of the meetings held by local authorities in Ilok and in one excerpt your name is mentioned. A certain F. Leko is the person who mentions your name. And he says there: "Does Grahovac know that Hadzic has stated that, regardless of the negotiations we are conducting, that he will level Ilok." I'm interested in knowing whether you ever stated something like this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't, nor could I have levelled Ilok or shot from any sort of weapons. I think that this is a mistake, but I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the Croats often mentioned my name as Adzic without the initial letter and Blagoje Adzic's name as Hadzic, I saw that often, but I never heard that Blagoje Adzic stated something like this. So I think that it's a clear case of misinformation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to hear from anyone that they heard about such a statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I heard about this the first time here in the courtroom, when I saw it on paper in this document. But, otherwise, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in Ilok or in the surrounding area when the Croats were moved out of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. Either in Ilok or in the surrounding area. And I did not have any information about this, any direct information, except for what I learned from the media. And when they asked me about this, I said what I had heard in the media. I didn't want to say that no one reported anything to me. I, rather, feigned that I did know something about it, even though actually I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you or the government enter Ilok or go to Ilok after the Croats had moved out? Did you establish any organs of SBWS there at the time in this territory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't establish any organs of power or authorities. We did not have physical access at the time. We couldn't reach it. There was military administration in Ilok. It was completely sealed off. I know why this was so, why they wouldn't allow me to come there and why the military administration was so strictly enforced. Let me explain. Ilok was at the far east of the Vukovar municipality. It was in a wedge surrounded by the border with Serbia. All the shops that existed there, the goods were all stored at one place so that it would be distributed from Ilok to surrounding villages because transportation from Ilok was expensive. And once military rule was introduced, everything was closed down for civilian authorities because economy was strong in Ilok. There was a winery and so on. And then all the material resources, all the official vehicles, everything that was in depots, even the gravel and the sand that was held there in storages, they moved everything to Serbia, and only after they had done all that, several months later, they agreed to hold talks with us. I just heard accidentally that an official vehicle that was used by the Ilok winery - it was an Opel Omega, that's what I was told - and that a JNA officer took off civilian licence plates on the bridge leading to Ilok, put on military licence plates and drove it off. And we were shocked because it was a kind of simple theft. Worse than looting. I'm not sure how I should call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have had a chance to hear Witness GH-168, and I wanted to ask you a few questions about certain parts of his statement. He claimed, inter alia, that there were staffs of a Territorial Defence unit in Ilok which was not organised by the JNA but by the military and political leadership of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 8337 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is: Are you aware of organs of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem organising units and staffs of Territorial Defence in the territory of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be aware of this because it's not true. They couldn't even get there physically, let alone do anything there. So this is completely fabricated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you appoint or head any body that appointed the commanders of the local Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a different matter. Neither myself nor any part of the government ever appointed a single TO Staff Commander, not a single one, including the one in Ilok. There was no physical access to Ilok, and even had there been physical access, no appointments would have been made by us. It was all done by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P378. It is tab 1258.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a report issued by the military command of the town of Ilok drafted on 9 December 1991. In item 1, it is stated that in Ilok and the villages of Sarengrad, Mohovo, Opatovac, Lovas, and Bapska, thus far, no civilian authorities had been formed. Does this reflect the real situation in that area? Do you know if there were any civilian organs in these settlements?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any. I don't think there were any. Although I wasn't present there at the time. We did not establish any. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In item 2, we can see the following: In the territory of the command of the town, there are no TO Staffs. Does that reflect the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Item 3, it is stated that there is a police station that was established in Ilok, and one of its squads -- or, actually, a detachment was sent to Lovas. And it is now under the authority of the SAO Baranja, Slavonia, and Western Srem. In carrying out its tasks, the police station is subordinated to the command of the town of Ilok. It is stated therein that a Serbian MUP established a police station but that it was the -- under the authority of the SAO Baranja, Slavonia, and Western Srem, yet carrying out the orders of the Ilok Town Command and subordinated to it. Can you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a triple degree of lack of logic, so to speak. I didn't even know who established that police station and under whose command it was. It had nothing to do with the government. Perhaps they were trying to say that they were on some payment list in the SAO of Baranja. But when they say that were under somebody's authority, it doesn't mean much to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think he is trying to say that you were supposed to pay those people working in the station?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it reminds me of that, that someone else commands them and yet that we or another body were supposed to pay them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the SBWS government pay the people working in that police station, if you knew, or did it pay out salaries to the people working in any other police stations in the area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, our budget was still in its infancy and we couldn't have afforded to pay anyone, let alone these people. They were established by the Serbian MUP, as far as I could learn later, they were all employed by the Serbian MUP and that's where probably they received their salaries. This is something I learned much later, as did most of the people present in this courtroom. I didn't know it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, were you in Lovas when the incident involving a minefield took place, as described in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. In 1991, I did not go to Lovas, not once. I didn't know about the incident at the time. I only heard of it much, much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Ljuban Devetak; and, if so, how long?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Ljuban Devetak. I've known him since late 1991 or early 1992, because I remember that he came to Erdut once, although I don't remember when any longer. I know him from the period before I became president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. So after 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government of the SBWS appoint him as town commander in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I explained how it worked. Town commanders were appointed by the inhabitants and TO commanders by the army. I didn't even hear of Ljuban Devetak being the town commander, and the government never discussed it. When I discussed village guards, perhaps those people who were in charge of their shifts could have been called town commanders, but that was in July and August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will need a more precise answer, I'm afraid, because the term "town commander" is a rather specific one. I think you referred to defence commander before, so I wanted to check with you whether you make a distinction between the two terms, town commander and defence commander, and were you now talking about town commander in that sense, or did you have in mind defence commander?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a mistake. It is very similar in my language. I had in mind the defence commanders in villages as formed in mid-1991, the village guards. As for town commanders and TO commanders, they had to do with these documents I saw at some later stage who were appointed by the JNA. I apologise for having made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, the crime in Lovas which is part of the indictment, was it investigated by anyone from SBWS or perhaps from another body like the JNA or the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime took place within the area of responsibility of the JNA. At the time it was there. I didn't know about it at the time, and I don't know if someone investigated it. I wasn't even aware of it. Later on, I learned that it was investigated by security organs from the JNA. I also learned that proceedings were instituted against the direct perpetrators in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that on 9 November 1991, TO members and policemen of the SBWS, as well as members of Arkan's unit, arrested and took Hungarians and Croats from Erdut, Dalj Planina, and Erdut Planina and took them to the training centre in Erdut, killing 12 of them in the process. That is contained in paragraph 27 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a few days later members of the Serb national security, together with Arkan, killed seven Hungarians? That's in paragraph 28 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have seen from the annex to the indictment that reference is made to several members of the Bence family, Pap family, and Senasi. Did you know any of them personally?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was even friends with the entire Pap family. They were very good friends of mine. And I also knew the brother of one of the witnesses who appeared here, but I knew him under the nickname Sobonja [phoen]. He owned a restaurant at Dalj Planina, Dalj mountain, and I often went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the Pap family is concerned, who were friends of yours, when did you find out that something had happened to them, they were no longer there, that they might have come to a bad end?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that in 1992. I can't say exactly where, but it was warm, so it could have been spring or summer 1992. Together with my friends, I was on my way to Dalj Planina to go to that restaurant. It turned out to be closed, and I asked passers-by what had come of them. And by the way, I didn't know them under their family name, Pap. I knew them under their nicknames. And that restaurant was called Saran. I was told that the father of the family and one of the sons got killed in the war, whereas the mother and another son were refugees in Osijek. I was shocked, and I said: Which son is alive and which is dead? And I was told that Ferika, the taller one, was killed and Nisi, the younger one, was still alive. And then I was shocked and very saddened when I heard from the witness here in court that all of them are actually dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see in the record that you were on your way to the restaurant with some friends of yours. Is that exactly what you said? I seem to have heard something different.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said with my escorts. The other one that I thought was alive, his -- his nickname was Misi, not Nisi, and his name was Misika.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if anybody investigated those incidents from back then or did you maybe learn later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it was in the area of responsibility of the JNA, I know that the JNA conducted an investigation or was supposed to conduct it. But obviously they didn't do it very well because the perpetrators were never found.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 59 of the indictment, reference is made to the crime in Klisa on 11 November 1991. Do you know anything about the arrests of these people from Klisa? Do you know anything about the incident? What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you all I know about that incident, but it was only a ten years later that I really learned what had happened, and I heard the details only here in The Hague during witness evidence. Towards the end of 1991, on the 11th November 1991, I came from Novi Sad to Erdut sometime in the morning, at least I think it was before noon, and when I repacked and got out of the car, the driver told me three men who were standing to the side were looking for me, along with a fourth man who was not from Klisa, unlike the first three. And among them was a man whom they knew. He worked as a car mechanic in Erdut. Those three men, I knew them. I knew they were from Klisa. I had played football with them earlier. They asked me if I was able to assist them because they had a report that some people who had been in the fields doing their farm work - as I thought then - had been arrested. Later I learned that they were actually arrested somewhere near their workplace. And these men also said that this could have been done by Arkan's Men, and I said -- I thought, in fact, that they were not able to go there where Arkan's Men were based. From the place where we were talking, there was only 100 yards to the gate of their base, and I said: Wait for me. I'll go there. I literally ran to that gate along with my escort, and when I came to the gate, I saw Arkan in the yard, and there were two guards standing at the gate. And as soon as I came in, I asked him if he knew anything about any arrests in Klisa, if he had any information at all. He seemed very nervous and upset, which I couldn't understand at the time. He said: Why does everyone blame me for everything? I'm not the police. I have nothing to do with arrests. I said: I didn't say you arrested them. I'm just asking if you have any information. And he said: Why are you asking me? Look. The holding cells are right here. That's where I put my soldiers when they get drunk and rowdy. The door is open. Why don't you look for yourself. And I said: Why would I look? I'm just asking you if you know anything or not. And he answered: I have to deal with such cases when somebody is holding themselves out to be Arkan's Men falsely. I'm fed up with this. I'll screw somebody's mother because of these false accusations. Half of my men are busy on the ground just arresting those people who are misrepresenting themselves. And then he asked: Who told you this? But I realised those men would be in trouble if I told him who they were, so I just left it there. I said: Okay. If you don't know anything. And I left. I went back to those three men and told them those people were not in Arkan's base. One of them was called Ormaz [phoen] and another was called Rajko. Just before this trial, my wife went to Klisa to find these men and to ask them if they would be willing to appear as witnesses and tell this story. Because we have some friends who had been in contact with them. This Rajko and Ormaz said they were not there but Mile Coralic [phoen] was certainly there. And they also think Mile Pavlovic and some man called Uzelac was also there. However, both Pavlovic and Uzelac live in Serbia. They had left Croatia. Of course, my wife got in touch with them too and they say, yes, Mile Coralic and Rajko and Ormaz were in that group, not them. So I found myself in a vicious circle. I was not able to bring witnesses to talk about this. Those who live in Serbia say they were not there, and the men who are still in Croatia also deny, and I don't understand why they are denying that they were there. Anyway, I told those men what I had found out and went towards that place where the government seat was, and then I saw Djordje Cukovic, who was a friend of mine also from Klisa. And I said in passing, those people are not held by Arkan. I forgot one more thing. Arkan said to me: Why you are looking for them? They are Ustashas. They must have defected to the Croatian side, walking across the fields. Which seemed very improbable to me. And I told Cukovic that those people were not held by Arkan because I knew he was from Klisa. I then went into my office where some people were waiting to have a meeting with me. When out from the canteen came Mica Panisic, who was the manager of an enterprise called Dalj. I was not on very good terms with them. In fact, we were not on speaking terms at all. He was talking and making a racket. I didn't hear what he was saying, and I wasn't going to stop to listen. I didn't even know that he was the manager of those people because I didn't make the connection. Dalj and Klisa are not so close to each other. I didn't realise there was any connection between him and them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you do that after the break, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I -- I do my best to do it during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Is this -- is this a convenient moment for the first break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a response to Mr. Stringer's question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'll give this response, although that I think that it is not appropriate moment for such kind of inquiry during the direct examination of the witness. Because it could be the subject of the separate submission, what was the subject of my cross-examination of some of the Prosecution witnesses. But now I'll give the reference. It is page 1457, line 13, to 1458, line 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Simply to say, Mr. President, I don't know that that in fact does -- what was put at those pages of the transcript in our view does not satisfy Rule 90(H). But on that point, I think I would agree with counsel, that it's probably left to -- unless the Chamber wishes to inquire further into it, it may be that we'll be directing the Chamber to what we view are other situations already where parts of witness statements have now been disputed with versions that were not put to the witnesses, and we are likely to make some form of a submission to identify all of those for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, were you present in Borovo Komerc on the 19th of November, 1991, when the Croatian forces surrounded -- surrendered themselves?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you come to the school in Borovo Selo that evening?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know a man called Ivan Baranjek?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him, and I never heard that last name in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was another witness here who talked about a man called Dragutin Susto?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is P2990, paragraph 57, page 70. Unfortunately, I have no tab for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, for the record, Mr. Zivanovic, the document number you cited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: P2990. Thank you. And you have no tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 669.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab 669. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One Dragutin Susto is mentioned here as your boss. Please tell me whether you knew this person and whether he was, indeed, your boss.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him, and he was not my boss. This is a generally known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you hear of Vukovar's fall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the 18th of November, when it actually fell, when it was broadcast in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you undertake any measures after that as the prime minister of the SBWS government and did the government do anything?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I didn't have any contact with the events in Vukovar, and that goes for the government as well. We had no contact with the so-called Operations Group South. However, since we presented ourselves as the SBWS government, it was necessary for us to show up in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to Vukovar before it fell while there was combat?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have described already, since I had fled Vukovar in early May, when I crossed the Danube with my daughter, and until the 20th of November, I did not return to Vukovar once. Not only Vukovar but the entire area that was covered by the Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry, it is tab 124.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is tab 124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a press conference or a statement by you given to journalists. Apparently you said that during the mopping up of terrain in Vukovar, it was reported that not a single house was left undamaged in Vukovar and that life was not possible there at that time. Can you tell us how you knew that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about it through -- from the media and through some conversations with the ministers who had some information, like I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall a government session held after the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, in general. Wherever sessions were held before that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a government session in Erdut on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, L38.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have had occasion to see these minutes. You recall it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: If you look at the heading and the first sentence, I can see that the meeting was held in Erdut and, in brackets, we can see Dalj. Can you explain to us, since I saw that in some other documents as well, why we can find Dalj there, whereas the session was actually held in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see that it says: Dalj, the 20th of November. Whereas the session was actually in Erdut on the 19th. It means that the minutes were drafted in Dalj given the fact that the government secretary had his office in Dalj as there were no adequate premises in Erdut. He actually transcribed the minutes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see the names of those present. It is also stated that Ilija Kojic was not present at the session. Do you know why he was absent?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija had been seriously wounded in early October and did not participate in any further sessions of the SBWS government. He was physically unable to, as he was in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at item 2, please. It is at the bottom of the original and on page 3 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see that you briefed those present about the current situation at international level and the talks held with the representatives of the Republic of Serbia and the JNA. Can you recall a bit more specifically what was the topic of your presentation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I always briefed the government following any of my meetings. I think a day or two before that I had consultations with a JNA general - I think his name is Slavko Jovic - who acquainted me with the Blue Helmets and the UN, in a manner of speaking, and then I conveyed that to the government and any potential Serbian representatives I met, such as the people I met with regard to my participation in international negotiations. I call them experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned General Jovic, can you tell us who it was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think by the time he had retired although I'm not certain. He was a head of mission of -- a UN mission, I think in Egypt. He had some diplomatic experience which is rather different from most officers, and he talked to us about that. I think Milan Babic was with me as well, although I'm not sure. He explained some things regarding the UN to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why were you interested in the subject of the UN at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that time, there was already mention of Blue Helmets who were to -- supposed to come and maintain peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the next page in the original and the last page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Item 5. We see there one of the conclusions reached by the government, which is that the JNA units were to be subordinated to the government in its territory. Can you tell us why that conclusion was made. What was the government trying to achieve by doing so?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in the field was the other way around. The JNA did not ask us anything, did not recognise us, and we could exert no influence over the JNA. There was a proposal that we reach that decision, but it was wishful thinking. We couldn't have implemented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence of item 3, you are cited as telling government members that due to the situation in Vukovar, it was necessary for the members of the government to be present there on the 20th of November and that the next government session would be convened on the 22nd November in Beli Manastir. Can you tell us why did you recommend to the members of government to come to Vukovar on the 20th of November, since the government session was to follow only a couple of days later, on the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to show up in Vukovar at any cost, so to say. In a way, we were being obstructed by the inhabitants and fighters of Vukovar who did not recognise the government with the support of some their war-time comrades from the JNA who said that the government did nothing to liberate Vukovar. In a way, they were telling us that we weren't welcome there. That is why I invited members of the government, those who wished to do so, to appear there, and we were all to go there at our own risk. That is why a session of the government had been planned to take place on the 22nd of November, even before Vukovar fell. It was the -- the plan was to show up in Vukovar. That was the only reason to make an appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: A Prosecution expert, Theunens, said something on pages 4616 and 4617 of the transcript. He stated that as of the 20th of November, the government was the main body establishing civilian authority over the District of SBWS while the JNA played a side role, or, as he put it, a supporting role. I was -- I would be interesting in finding out if that is correct and what role did the government have in establishing civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is incorrect. We only began establishing civilian authorities as of that date, but on that date, nothing had been established. There was military rule for a month, two, or even three months, in the most easterly part of the district following that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, D19. It is tab 1335.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The expert relied on this document, in particular, to state that. We see that the date is the 20th of November, 1991. Please have a look at paragraph 2, or item 2. I'm interested in one part of that paragraph, which is rather sizeable. It is stated that town commands were supposed to work on establishing civilian authorities in municipalities, in brackets: "(According to the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian District of Baranja, Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem. The municipalities are Beli Manastir, Vukovar, Dalj, Vinkovci with its seat in Mirkovci, and Osijek with its seat in Tenja)." Do you remember when that decision was reached establishing these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that I'm in a very delicate situation here and I have to stand by every single word I say, I believe, although I'm not sure 100 per cent, this decision was made only later. At this time, I didn't know myself that the territorial division would be this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, L42.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first paragraph of this decision, you can see the date when this regulation was enacted.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was enacted on 21 November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see next page, both in B/C/S and English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at Article 11, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that Article 11, which straddles the next page, lists all populated areas that make part of certain municipalities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's five municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we go back to D19. It is 1335, tab 1335. [Interpretation] We can move to the last page in B/C/S and in English. Sorry, page 2 in B/C/S and page 2 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see in item 6, the last line in B/C/S and the last-but-one in the English translation, this government commissioner for Vukovar is named. It is Srbobran Bibic. Can you tell us, did the government have a commissioner for Vukovar at the time, and if so, was he called Bibic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the government did not have a commissioner for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government appoint Mr. Bibic to any other position, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only on the 20th November when I came to Vukovar that I began consultations concerning Mr. Bibic and the possibility that he become president of the Executive Council of Vukovar. So if the consultations started on the 20th, I don't know if it was done towards the end of November or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please L43. It is tab 1209.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see in this text that on 28 November, the government of the Serbian district passed the decision to appoint Srbobran Bibic as president of the Executive Council of Vukovar municipality. Is this the decision?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. So it was passed on the 28th of November. We only confirmed what was already a fact, where Boro Zivanovic was in Baranja and they were working independently of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how the JNA was able to foresee some of your decisions that hadn't been adopted yet; namely, this decision that the government made only on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can think of is that it was back-dated. They couldn't have known it at that time. This document was written later. Although that document contains a lot of inaccuracies. They call our government the government of SAO Krajina and -- based in Erdut, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to all the information we have, on the 20th of November, you did go to Vukovar. So I'd like to ask you: How did you reach Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I travelled to Vukovar via Backa Palanka and via Ilok, I think, or perhaps Sid; I cannot remember exactly. The roads go in parallel for a certain length and then they join at Sotin. But I came to Vukovar from the side of Sotin because it was impossible to go there from the side of Borovo Naselje, which I realised only later. There was still fighting in Borovo Naselje. I remember I reached Vukovar from that side, from Mitnica, and we were shocked. It was the first time I entered the town after three months. There were three beautiful houses just at the entrance. I knew the owner of one of them. We were in the karate club together. All the three houses had been torched. We knew that there had been fighting in Vukovar, but only then did we realise on what scale the destruction was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was with you when you travelled to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Japundzic was the driver. I was in the front passenger seat, and in the back seat were Ljubomir Mudrinic and Dr. Savo Stupar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what time it was approximately when you arrived at Vukovar? Specifically Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, it was between 1.00 and 2.00 p.m., in the early afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember any other members of your government who came to Vukovar then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember Vitomir Devetak, Dr. Mladen Hadzic, Vojin Susa, the President of the Assembly, Ilija Koncarevic, and Ilija Petrovic must have been there, although I can't remember him, because they always went together. And there were certainly others, but I can't remember them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember anyone else who was there, apart from members of your cabinet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Vojnovic, president of the court; Minister for Agriculture, Slavko Dokmanovic; Assistant Minister for Information, Rade Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone meet you at Velepromet? Did you talk to anyone? Were there any military authorities there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, nobody met us. The courtyard was full of civilians who were milling about. We didn't run into any problems of the kind we had feared, and it was only later that a lieutenant-colonel showed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said you feared some specific problems. What kind of problems?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that session of the cabinet that was held the day before, I heard some threats were issued from Vukovar, and we were supposed to travel on the 19th but then we decided to postpone it. But I said I would go on the next day anyway, and the rest of the people could decide for themselves. There were even threats that they would physically liquidate us if we come, because they had a grudge against us because we had disappointed their expectations that we would help, although there was no way we could do anything to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened when that lieutenant-colonel appeared?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We filed together into a room that could be used, although it was inadequate. It was a small room with school desks and very small chairs for junior school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I greeted him, I kissed him, because we hadn't seen each other for a couple of months, and if this is interesting, he is the young man in the image which was showed in the beginning, where I have the moustache and we're at a wedding party. We were good friends, and I think that this photograph is now part of the evidence and perhaps it's not so important, but anyway. So perhaps after 1500 hours, 1530, I left Velepromet and I went in the direction of Sid, that is to say, Serbia. There were five of us in the car on the way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you return with the same persons you had come with, plus one more person, or was it different now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same persons with the addition of Darko Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you will remember that you testified as a witness in the Slavko Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D3565, please. It is -- it is tab 1407.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember that you testified as a witness before this Tribunal in the Slavko Dokmanovic case?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I testified via videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we go to the page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your testimony, you said that the meeting was chaired by a lieutenant-colonel who introduced himself as the town commander. Today you shared his name with us. Why did you not mention his name back then? Was there a reason?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I wasn't 100 per cent certain. Once he showed up in the courtroom, I realised that was the person. Even in Novi Sad when I saw him in the cafe, had he not introduced himself, I would not have recognised him, and that was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see in the transcript that it was later. When later?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I testified in the Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At page 25 of the same transcript, you testified that there was discussion at the meeting about the prisoners but that you were not competent to deal with it. Can you clarify, what were you trying to say when you said that you had no authority or no competence to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been 15 years since that testimony so I no longer remember precisely. However, the lieutenant-colonel told us that he was not authorised to discuss it. If your question goes to our authority, we simply had no resources for such a large number of prisoners. But as for the ten to 15 people I referred to, we had proof that they had committed crimes and wanted to have them tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 26, you said that neither you nor the government had no military role to play in the SBWS. In what sense? What did you mean when you said that you had no military role?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat what I said back then. We couldn't order anything to the JNA or even to agree with them on -- on any issue. It was all under their competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the clock, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. We'll take the second break. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, when the meeting was finished and when you left Vukovar, you provided an interview for TV Belgrade in Sid; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1731, tab 390. We just need transcripts. Sorry, 1731. P1731.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the transcript of the interview. I would kindly ask you to answer a few questions that have to do with what was stated therein. First of all, you said that a government session had been held in Vukovar. In today's testimony, you said it was not a session. First of all, did you, indeed, say that in the interview - in other words, is the text of the interview correct - and, secondly, is that correct in terms of whether it was a government session or it wasn't?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I said that there had been a government session but it is incorrect that it, indeed, took place. However, I did say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we move on, you have had occasion to read the -- through the text of the interview and even see the footage. Is what is transcribed here accurate? Does it reflect what you said back then so that I don't need to go through each and every sentence with you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it actually reflects my words at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Next, you said that the government concluded that those with blood in their -- on their hands cannot leave the territory of the SBWS and that they can only be tried by the people. Was that a conclusion made by the government?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not a government conclusion. And the government was not quorate to discuss it. That was not even discussed at the meeting, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Next we find that you apparently reached an agreement with the military authorities to leave the Ustasha in "our camps in the environment of" -- "in the environs of Vukovar." Was this correct, you referring to the agreement with the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no agreement with the military authorities and what I said is incorrect. The only agreement there was, was to have a bread truck sent the next day because the remaining population had -- did not have bread. That was the only agreement. There was no other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any camps in the environs of Vukovar at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The government was unaware of the existence of any camps in the environs of Vukovar. What I heard about later referred to JNA camps, and I learned of it subsequently, several years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean specifically?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The event at Ovcara as well as the camps in Serbia that I heard about later, save for Sremska Mitrovica, I didn't know of any other camps, such as Stajicevo, Begejci, and Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can only -- we can also find that you stated that the people who were taken to Mitrovica were to be returned by you, that you took upon yourself to have them returned, if they could be called people in the first place. Can you explain that sentence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It concerned 15 to 20 people of whom we knew had committed serious war crimes. Even back then, as now, I was unable to call them people, no matter what ethnic group they belonged to. A day or two prior to the interview, I saw an interview taken by a TV journalist whose name is Milena Gabanelli who said she saw slaughtered Serb children in a kindergarten in Borovo Naselje whose fingers had been cut off and that some Croatian soldiers made necklaces with those fingers. Later on it proved to be false information and I don't know who launched it and why. I had in mind those specific people when I said that they should be tried and that they could not be referred to as people, although they were members of the homo sapiens species. But there was information going around, there was a story, which I managed to prove untrue, that in the village of Mirkovci, a basket of eyes was found who had been gouged out by Croats from Serbs in the house owned by the person called Ivan Odor [phoen]. At first when I heard that I was upset, but then I said: People, I went to school with him, and when we played football in Marinci as guests, I had dinner in his family house and I met his parents. I told them that it couldn't be true, that somebody lied. So I was quite cautious in terms of accepting misinformation. I did think that the Italian journalist Milena Gabanelli would be neutral. In any case, I had about five or six names at the time out of a total of 15 to 20 who should have been tried by our court. I don't know how visible it is in my statement but I did say that these people should be tried and I did cite two types of court we had, the municipal and district one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further in the text, you say that 3.000 members of Croatian forces surrendered. Tell us how you came up with that number and whether it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that number is the most telling about how serious it all was. The government did not have its own intelligence service, and in our contacts with military authorities in Vukovar, we were unable to get that information. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic said nothing about it, and I believe he didn't know anything. I was just saying nonsense. There couldn't have been even a third of that number of active-duty troops in Vukovar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said at one point that you were much more optimistic before you got to Vukovar. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that I said that and that's what I was thinking. I had imagined that at least something in Vukovar was intact. At that time, I could not imagine - and probably you can't imagine it now - that not a single thing in Vukovar was left standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned you were in contact with people from Petrova Gora who carried this battle through, and you mentioned in your previous testimony Mr. Jaksic, and you said you went, yourself, to Petrova Gora. Did you see Miroljub Vujovic there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him there. At that time, I didn't know the man. I had never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Stanko Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Milan Lancuzanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of this interview, you said it had been agreed not to impose military rule for a long time, just for a few days. Is that true? Did you, indeed, have such an understanding?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not have such an understanding. Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic said he wasn't even willing to discuss it with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, my inference from your evidence today is that this entire interview, everything you said in it, is untrue. Can you tell us what was the reason why you were saying all these untrue things?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I believe it's called the Machiavellian approach, from the Italian Niccolo Machiavelli. I thought that telling the truth would then result in a complete collapse of the system. Now I can tell you what the truth was. The army wasn't willing to talk to us at all about anything. The people from the Territorial Defence were threatening that they were going to destroy the government and that another SAO Vukovar would be formed, and it was very possible at that moment that another civilian authority would be established independent of our government. From talking to those people who were in the yard at the time, some of whom I knew, some not, I heard about various war crimes, and I was just saying those things to show them that the government cares and that we would pursue it and the perpetrators would be tried. I just wanted to diffuse tensions and prevent things from getting worse in terms of the relations between our Serb and Croat neighbours, to fend off any possible incidents. The real truth is that this interview has absolutely nothing in common with the situation on the ground. Could we now go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, could I make a proposal because it was -- it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- even before the break, we -- I think everyone forgot and we remained in private session during another phase of the evidence, and the Prosecution was going to propose lifting the private session or releasing that part. Perhaps the Prosecution and the Defence as well, the parties could suggest so the Chamber what parts of this recent statement could or should be released to the public, and then the Chamber could decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I had the same idea, Mr. Stringer. Thank you. And when could you let us know?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, shortly after today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Have you finished, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I noticed one transcript error. It is on page 55, line 16. I -- line -- line 19, the word "league." As far as I know, he -- it should be replaced with the word "legal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you have said that this interview you gave was misused. Can you tell me, to the best of your knowledge, who misused it, for what purpose, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Belgrade, a Commission for Co-ordination of the Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal was established, and this commission invited witnesses to be and told them what to say, for instance, to use the word "tractor" instead of "military vehicle," to say "civilian residents of Vukovar" instead of "the JNA," and I believe this abuse was perpetrated by the military security service and its chief, Aleksandar Vasiljevic. I think my interview was abused in the same way. I think you know by now yourselves that the military courts and military services coached the witnesses to lay the blame on the civilian authorities, which didn't even exist at the time, and deflect blame from the military and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can go back to the open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Open session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we will change the subject a bit, Mr. Hadzic. Among other things during the trial, we have heard a lot about refugees from Western Slavonia who were accommodated for a time in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Could you tell us, as we have the information that you, among others, invited people to find temporary accommodation there and that the accommodation for them was insured. Could you tell us how the need arose for these people to be possibly accommodated in SBWS and how their accommodation was organised? Who organised it, and what was the situation like in certain parts of the region?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the testimony of Witness Veljko Dzakula, we all heard about the tribulations of the people in Western Slavonia, how they suffered. These people came via Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia. Some of them stayed in Serbia, and perhaps one-third managed to reach SBWS. And it was spontaneous, rather than organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where these refugees who arrived to SBWS were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were accommodated in abandoned houses. Most of the abandoned houses were those that belonged to the Croats who had left the area, who had left -- or, rather, withdrawn together with the Croatian army, but there were also quite a number of empty Serbian houses where there were no Serbs. For example, in my village, there were several abandoned houses where they also found accommodation. So whichever house was empty and had some minimum conditions, that is to say, was not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that some people came to your village. Did they come to live in abandoned houses that used to belong to Serbs or Croats?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no abandoned Croatian houses in my village. All the Croats who had lived there before the war remained there, no one had any problems. But there were a number of abandoned Serb houses. There are some to this day. So that some who had been refugees returned and they still live in the village, but those who came, came from Vozuca in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where they suffered a lot from the Muslims rather than from the Croats. There were those from Western Slavonia as well, but I don't actually know because I haven't been living there for 15 years now. I think that there is one family from Western Slavonia living there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the houses were given over to the refugees so that they became the owners or were they allowed to use them for some specific time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this specific issue was not directly within my purview, but I know that it was temporary, and the decisions that we took were about putting up these people there temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether any records were kept about allowing refugees to move into those houses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that commissions were formed at the level of local communes from the information I had at that time, and I know that it was done in the most serious manner that it was possible at that time, but I don't remember much -- that in much greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see P110, please. It is tab 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an approval issued by the local commune or, rather, the Executive Council of the Dalj local commune on the 19th of November, 1991. It reads that a person is granted temporary occupancy of a house and it's described where the house is located. Can you tell us whether these were typical permissions or approvals that were issued at that time? If you know.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see it now here, but I didn't come across that at the time. But I believe that this would be the appropriate thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P275.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. It is tab 221 [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a decision from Erdut issued in early 1992 about granting something for occupancy. Can you tell us whether this was also the typical decision issued at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
