utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. I see the signature, and one witness here said that her husband was the chairman of the commission, and I am familiar with the last name that we can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that, likewise, land was granted to some of the refugees who arrived in the area at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen that in documents here now, but I wasn't familiar with that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D197.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is 734. [Interpretation] Can we please move on to the next page. [In English] Sorry ... [Interpretation] And one more, please. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is quite an extensive document with lots of pages. But can you see here that we have a register of persons who were granted land, and the land itself, where it is located, and everything else? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also see that under number 3 is the husband of one of the witnesses who was a Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So he was granted land or ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that land was granted to him. I didn't know it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether a ministry within the government dealt with this issue granting land for temporary use and the records of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with this, so I don't really know. This, under number 3, could have been the husband's brother, but, in any case, they were Croats. This is what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P1818.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It is tab 410. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask you to look at the first paragraph of this report. It is relevant, in a way, for what we are discussing right now. Please tell me whether this description of events with regard to the refugees from Western Slavonia corresponded with the information you had at the time about those events?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it corresponded. I'm not certain now. I know that chaos reigned there and that the Croats had expelled the Serbs there from the Serbian villages, and that threatened by force, they had left the villages. But I have to note that that was in Western Slavonia, and I was not present in that area at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. It may be that this is a confidential exhibit and that we'd need to use a redacted version in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Not to be broadcasted, Madam Registrar. Would that be the solution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's use the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not marked as confidential. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is marked confidential, Mr. Zivanovic, Madam Registrar tells me. So out of an abundance of caution let's broadcast the redacted version. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think it was a 54 bis exhibit. And the redacted version is 1818.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's already on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, I wanted to ask you about your visit to Sremska Mitrovica which took place after the fall of Vukovar. You have heard various testimonies about that here, and I would ask you to tell us whether you went to visit the prison in Sremska Mitrovica; and if so, when, and what the purpose of your visit was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there perhaps ten or 15 days after these events, or later. After a couple of days, I requested from the secretary of the government to try and schedule my visit but it couldn't take place any earlier, so I went there in early December, if I remember properly. I don't know the exact date. I know that a visit of the delegation of the SBWS government was scheduled and also a delegation of the prosecutor's offices and court, together with the government. I came alone with drivers. And in front of the prison, I was met by Minister Susa and another minister and I think that one of the judges from Vukovar was with him there, and we then entered. We went to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone from the prison, a military or civilian person who was in charge of the prison? The prison warden or one of his assistants? Did you have a chance to do that on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I know that it was a civilian prison, but a section of it was occupied by the army and it was like a military prison. There was a colonel there whom I didn't know at the time. I later saw that here. I think that his last name was Maksimovic. So he was the host in a way. And the civilian warden or his deputy were also in the delegation but no one asked them anything. They just welcomed me there. There were some other military policemen or non-commissioned officers there. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to the people who welcomed you, in particular, that colonel and possibly the other military personnel? Was there any discussion and what was it about? What was it like, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that there was any discussion. I don't think so. But I believe that my visit, the visit of our delegation, would be the first step and that later on, after that, co-operation would be continued. So I saw it as a sort of step that was to break the ice or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "co-operation" after that, in what sense do you mean this? What kind of co-operation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were ready to provide them with the information that we had in connection with the investigations and possibly the trials. As it was no longer possible for them to hand anyone over to us so that these people could be put on trial in SBWS, or at least that was how I then understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it made possible to enter the prison itself, to see the people detained there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Following this regular procedure, it was made possible for us. We had to hand over all our weapons and then we were allowed to enter, as we would have been in any other prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who were the members of the group that entered the prison?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the two people who escorted me, Vojin Susa, the justice minister, and Boro Bogunovic, the police minister, I think, and there was somebody from the court in Vukovar and the prosecutor's office, but I don't know who. There were also representatives of the military authorities in the prison, the colonel I mentioned and the deputy civilian warden. I think there were up to some ten of us in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which parts of the prison did you visit and what were you able to see once you were inside?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to recall. As the president of the republic, I did go back once or twice in 1993 because some of our inmates from the Republic of Serbian Krajina were detained there, serving their sentences. In any case, I remember that we only went into one building and went up to the first floor. I think the building has two floors in total. They took us to a room to see. I remember it was a large one with perhaps around 100 people in it, maybe slightly less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you enter the room? Did you talk to the people who were accommodated in there, the inmates?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went in a few steps only. I greeted them but did not comment any further. I did recognise some of my friends and acquaintances, and I wasn't feeling very well. It wasn't pleasant. Those I knew, I believe they had no place to be there, and I also supposed that the rest, the people I didn't know, were not supposed to be there, given the fact that none of the people who were on our list was there -- were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you offer any comment on that occasion? Did you say something to the people who were escorting you, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, I think I told those people: Okay. Everything will be fine, and as far as I know there will be no problems. It was a humane way to address them. I asked the colonel, I think, why these people were being held in the first place. So it was a humane comment to make, but it was very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you visited the area with the inmates, did you go to any other areas where there were other inmates?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I was going up the stairs, I did see some detainees turned with their backs to me, facing the wall. I don't know why they were made to stand that way. There was a military policeman next to each one of them with their white belts. The people who were detained had their hands behind their back, and it was very unpleasant. I had experienced much the same situation back when I was arrested at Plitvice. We climbed up and went to a classroom or, actually, I think they called it library, or reading room. I asked there whether any Serbs were detained. I was interested in knowing that. They said there was a Serb who had been a policeman and who, by sheer circumstance, remained on the Croatian side. I asked if I could see him. It seems that he was quite near on the stairs and approached me. We shook hands and sat at the table. I asked him a normal thing that was at the time as would be for any people on the other side. I asked him whether this or that person was alive, whether they were in Zagreb, whether they were engaged in the war, et cetera. I didn't ask specifically, but I think I mentioned Darko Bekic, a friend of mine, inquiring if he knew of his fate. I also asked him about his well-being at the time. I don't even remember his name any longer. I just remember that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Emil Cakalic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in person. But I did know of his first and last name. He was a municipal inspector in charge of sanitation and hygiene measures. I didn't even know he was a Croat. I always took him for a Serb. I didn't recognise his last name as a Croatian one, and I didn't even know he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Ljubomir Pribudic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I saw him here in the courtroom for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you interrogate any detainees while you were visiting the jail -- the prison?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not interrogate anyone. And I was together with the rest of the delegation all the time. I did not separate. Even when I spoke to the Serb from the police force we were seated at the table, but the rest of the delegation was around us and everyone could hear what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You could read what Cakalic said to the effect that you beat him at the time when you visited Sremska Mitrovica. Can you comment upon that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said that Boro Savic and I beat him. That is incorrect. I didn't even see him, and I didn't know that he was in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was Boro Savic in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is why I found it strange when he said that Boro Savic and I beat him. I have no idea where that came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You could also hear Pribudic's testimony who also claimed that you beat him in Sremska Mitrovica. Can you comment upon that testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is untrue, of course. I don't know where it came from. I feel very unpleasant. He is an elderly, sick man. I don't know why he said it. He must have been mistake. I feel the urge to say something to the Court in full responsibility being aware of possible consequences. Since this is publicly broadcast and somebody is watching in Serbia and Croatia, Your Honour, I don't know whether it heard it from anyone else before but never in my life did I hit anyone. It may sound unlikely but I never even slapped anybody or struck anyone with a fist. Even in sports match -- matches, I always had the opportunity to stop myself from hitting anyone. If someone having listened to me now showed up and said that I ever hit him, I would be willing to face them and address that. I never hit anyone. Unless we go all the way back before I was even 10 years old. But in the last 45 years I never had an argument with anyone, let alone a fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've had occasion to see a letter sent by Colonel Maksimovic to Colonel Gligorevic; P3200.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see here that you were there on a visit on the 10th of December, 1991. Does that tally?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It is possible that it was on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Without quoting the entire letter now, since you have had an opportunity to see it as it is in evidence, but were you or any member of your delegation coming into conflict with the officers of the JNA who were there, including Colonel Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. While I was there, communication was very decent. There were no arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Vojin Susa said, on that occasion, that he would bring his own armed crew which was to take part in the work alongside the military?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that in my presence; and, as far as I know, he did not have any such armed crew, nor could anyone enter the premises armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you or anyone from your entourage threaten Aleksandar Vasiljevic at the time, or did anyone tell those present that they could easily be left without their general?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear any -- anything of the sort and I'm not aware of it being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were there with the delegation, was there any exchange of words with Colonel Maksimovic, an argument, to the effect that you wanted something that he did not want to provide for you? Was there a confrontation with him or any other representatives of the military?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we began discussing this topic, I did mention that it was supposed to have been an ice-breaking meeting, and we ended the meeting on that note. There was no confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did your visit last?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long. Perhaps half an hour or maybe up to 45 minutes. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you all leave together, or did you stay behind? Did anyone else stay behind? How did you say your goodbyes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all left the enclosed part of the prison together, and we went to the civilian area with free access. Then we went out onto the street, we said goodbye, and I left with my drivers. I don't know where the others went to. Perhaps we went for a lunch. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, we'll adjourn for the day. You won't forget you're still a witness and under oath. Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
